name: V-taper / shoulder-to-waist ratio

lead: A V-taper is a torso wide at the shoulders and upper back that narrows to a small waist, giving an inverted-triangle silhouette. It is a long-standing bodybuilding ideal and a standard frame goal in looksmaxxing, often written as a shoulder-to-waist ratio of about 1.6, tied to the golden ratio.

The ratio rises when the shoulders and upper back get wider or the waist gets smaller. Wider comes from deltoid and latissimus growth on top of the bone structure set by the clavicles; a smaller waist is mainly linked to body fat loss, and abdominal exercise alone is described as not enough to reduce waist girth. The 1.6 figure comes from bodybuilding culture; Wikipedia's waist-hip ratio article reports one study in which waist-to-chest ratio was the largest determinant of male attractiveness, and no studies of shoulder-to-waist ratio as a target were found.

paras: People train delts and lats, often with lateral raises, pull-ups and rows, while cutting body fat to narrow the waist. They track the ratio with a tape measure. Changes build over months of lifting and dieting.
The practice itself is ordinary training and dieting. Reported concerns are body-image fixation and skipping legs or overtraining while chasing a number. The 1.6 target is a cultural convention.

angle.text: Lifters and looksmaxxers aim for a shoulder-to-waist ratio near 1.6 by building the shoulders and back while cutting waist fat, producing an inverted-triangle silhouette. Muscle widens the top while fat loss narrows the middle. The 1.6 target is a forum and bodybuilding figure rather than a result from a specific attractiveness study.

lead: The V-taper is a physique in which broad shoulders and a wide upper back narrow down to a slim waist, producing an inverted-triangle silhouette. People pursue it to look broader and more athletic in clothes and out of them: the shoulders and back are built with resistance training, and the waist is kept narrow mainly through body-fat management. In looksmaxxing it is discussed as the shoulder-to-waist ratio (SWR), a frame metric that can be changed with gym work, unlike skeletal traits such as height [1][2].

A figure of about 1.6, linked to the golden ratio, is often quoted as the target. Grokipedia, an AI-generated source, attributes the figure to bodybuilding aesthetics and credits classic physiques such as Steve Reeves and later champions with popularising the look, although several of its citations for the attractiveness claims do not appear to match those claims [1]. Wikipedia's article on the golden ratio notes that many claimed appearances of the ratio in nature and art are disputed, so the number is better understood as a cultural convention in physique circles than a measured optimum [3].

Published research on body shape and attractiveness measures related ratios, mainly shoulder-to-hip ratio and waist-to-chest ratio, in rating and brain-imaging experiments. Findings are broadly that broader-shouldered, narrower-waisted male figures are rated as more attractive, with variation by population; these studies do not test a specific 1.6 target or whether training toward one changes outcomes [4][5][6][7][7][7].

paras: The V-taper is built from the deltoids, latissimus dorsi and trapezius on a skeletal base set by clavicle length, with a narrower waist coming from low body fat and limited oblique bulk [1]. These anatomical points are consistent with Wikipedia's descriptions of the deltoid, which gives the shoulder its rounded contour, and the clavicle, which sets shoulder breadth [8][9]. The latissimus dorsi is a large, fan-shaped muscle running from the lower spine, pelvis and lower ribs to the upper arm bone, and is the muscle most associated with a flared back [10].

The ratio is usually computed from either linear widths (shoulder width over waist width) or circumferences (shoulders around the deltoids over waist at the navel). Because the measurements differ between users, quoted ratios are not strictly comparable. In research, comparable constructs include shoulder-to-hip ratio and waist-to-chest ratio, the latter being the waist circumference divided by the chest circumference, so that a smaller value means a more V-shaped torso [4][7].

sections.h: Origins in bodybuilding and physique sport
paras: Modern bodybuilding grew out of strongman and physique-display shows in the late nineteenth century. Wikipedia credits the German-born Eugen Sandow, called the father of modern bodybuilding, with staging the first large bodybuilding contest, the Great Competition, at London's Royal Albert Hall on 14 September 1901 [11]. The IFBB's Mr. Olympia began in 1965 and became the sport's most prominent contest [11].

Steve Reeves, who won Mr. America in 1947, Mr. World in 1948 and Mr. Universe in 1950, is widely regarded as one of the most influential bodybuilders and was known for symmetry; he later became a film star in sword-and-sandal epics such as Hercules (1958) [12]. Grokipedia credits mid-twentieth-century classic physiques of this kind, and the 1970s Golden Era, with making the V-taper a standard ideal [1].

Two modern divisions put the shape at the centre of judging. Men's Physique, introduced in 2013 for athletes who found open bodybuilding too large, is judged mainly on front and back poses in board shorts. Classic Physique, added to the Mr. Olympia programme in 2016, is described by Wikipedia as emphasising symmetry, proportion and pleasing lines and valuing a small waist over size, with judges looking for a tapered torso in the vacuum pose; Chris Bumstead had won the title six times as of 2024 [11].

sections.h: Anatomy and how the shape is built
paras: Width at the top comes from the lateral deltoid, which adds shoulder breadth, and the latissimus dorsi, which flares the back below the armpits; the trapezius adds neck and upper-back mass [1][8]. Wikipedia lists vertical pulling movements such as pull-ups, chin-ups and pulldowns, along with straight-arm pulldowns, pullovers and rows, among the exercises that train the lats and surrounding muscles [10]. Bone structure sets a ceiling: clavicle length and shoulder-joint width differ between people and are not altered by training [9].

The waist component is mainly body fat. Wikipedia's abdominal exercise entry reports that a 2011 study found abdominal exercise alone did not reduce abdominal fat or girth, which is why practitioners pair training with fat loss and diet [13]. Some lifters also limit heavy direct oblique training on the argument that thicker obliques widen the waist; this is a practitioner view that Wikipedia's page does not address [1][13].

sections.h: The 1.6 target and the golden ratio
paras: The golden ratio, about 1.618, has long been invoked in aesthetics. Wikipedia's article notes that claims about its use by artists such as Leonardo da Vinci are not supported by his own writings, that a 1999 study of 565 paintings found no systematic use, and that many alleged examples in nature are considered fictitious; it also records that some twentieth-century artists, including Le Corbusier and Dalí, deliberately used it [3].

Within physique culture the ratio is tied to the proportions of classic champions, and posters compare their own measurements with it [1][2]. Neither the encyclopedia sources nor the research located here identifies 1.6 as a measured optimum for shoulder-to-waist ratio.

In looksmaxxing, the ratio is treated as a frame metric. Proponents say a high ratio signals masculinity, strength and health, and they discuss training shoulders, back and neck while keeping the waist small. Threads on looksmax.org ask which body parts to prioritise to achieve the shape, and post progress claims such as adding several inches to overall width in half a year of training [2][14].

A recurring argument is whether leg training harms the ratio. Some posters ask whether skipping legs improves the look; others in the same thread argue for training all muscle groups, including glutes and quads [2]. Neck training is also mentioned as a way to add upper-body width [2]. Other threads carry titles such as a request for 'fraud methods' for a wide-shoulder, small-waist look and a question about which body parts to focus on, and one thread pairs a V-taper body with a low facial rating [15][14][16]. These are community discussions rather than clinical findings.

Wikipedia's physical-attractiveness article states that a slim waist, broad shoulders and muscular chest are often found attractive, and summarises one study in which waist-to-chest ratio was the largest determinant of male attractiveness, with BMI and waist-to-hip ratio less significant. It adds that gay men in one study preferred a lower waist-to-chest ratio than straight men, and that Swami and Tovee found urban women in Britain and Malaysia weighted waist-to-chest ratio more heavily than rural women, who weighted BMI more [4][5].

In the 2005 Body Image study, which collected ratings from 95 women, waist-to-chest ratio was the main predictor of male attractiveness among urban British raters, while body mass index was the main predictor among rural Malaysian raters; urban raters preferred slimmer, more V-shaped figures [7]. A 2012 PLoS ONE study in which participants built ideal bodies with an interactive 3D program reported an ideal male body with a waist-to-chest ratio of about 0.74 in men's own choices and 0.77 in women's choices for a partner, with both BMI and torso shape contributing [7]. A 2005 study of Chinese and Caucasian men's bodies found that a volume-height index explained about 73 percent of the variance in ratings, with other ratios playing smaller roles [7].

More recent experiments in Archives of Sexual Behavior (2023) found that larger shoulder-to-hip ratios were judged more attractive than smaller ones by both men and women in an EEG study, and that across four studies with 659 heterosexual women, taller men and men with larger ratios were rated as more attractive, masculine and capable in a fight; how height and ratio interacted depended on the realism of the stimuli [7]. A 2013 PNAS study in which women rated life-size computer images of men found that the attractiveness effect of another physical trait varied with the men's height and shoulder-to-hip ratio [7]. A 2022 eLife meta-analysis of 96 studies reported that strength and muscularity were the strongest and the only consistent predictors of mating and reproductive outcomes among the male traits examined [7].

Grokipedia states that broad shoulders paired with a narrow waist signal dominance and that upper-body strength cues account for most variance in men's bodily attractiveness, but it supplies no sample sizes or methods and its citations appear weak [1].

Wikipedia describes muscle dysmorphia, a subtype of body dysmorphic disorder recognised in DSM-5 in 2013, as a belief that one's body is too small or insufficiently muscular despite a normal or large build; it reports estimates from 1 to 54 percent of men in sampled groups, with higher rates among gym members, weightlifters and bodybuilders [17]. Posters on looksmax.org do trade measured ratios and progress numbers [2]. The practice of training and dieting itself is ordinary exercise; the concerns noted are about fixation, overtraining and skipped sessions in pursuit of a number.

No studies found of training toward a 1.6 shoulder-to-waist ratio as an intervention. Related experiments are perception studies in which participants rate body images that vary in shoulder-to-hip or waist-to-chest ratio, summarised above [4][6][7][7][7]. A review of noninvasive body contouring in men also exists in the dermatology literature and concerns fat reduction and muscle toning devices rather than the V-taper as a target [18].

lore.intro: The V-taper is discussed as a core body goal on looksmax.org, with the ratio often posted and compared and with debate over leg training.[2]

claims.claim: A shoulder-to-waist ratio of about 1.6 is the ideal
A narrow waist comes from fat loss, not abdominal exercise
Skipping leg day improves the ratio
Broad shoulders with a narrow waist signal dominance and attractiveness
A V-taper can compensate for an unremarkable face.
Training toward a big ratio can become a fixation.
